nodes.name: Bulk Schrödinger equation of motion
nodes.statement: We consider\footnote{The natural units $\hbar =c=k_{\rm B}=1$ are adopted throughout the paper.} \begin{equation} \left (\ri \prt_t +\frac{1}{2m} \prt_x^2\right )\psi (t,x,i) = 0\, , \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Free Schrödinger dynamics for $\psi(t,x,i)$ along each lead.
nodes.section: 2.1 Particle current in the presence of defect

nodes.name: Boundary condition in the vertex
nodes.statement: with the boundary condition \begin{equation} \lim_{x\to 0^-}\sum_{j=1}^N \left [\eta (\II-\UU)_{ij} +\ri (\II+\UU)_{ij}\prt_x \right ] \psi (t,x,j) = 0\, , \end{equation} where $\UU$ is a $N\times N$ unitary matrix and $\eta \in \RR$ is a parameter with dimension of mass.
nodes.statement_short: Point-like defect encoded in a vertex boundary condition fixed by a unitary $\UU$ and a mass scale $\eta$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Particle current in the presence of defect

nodes.name: Parametrisation of all self-adjoint extensions
nodes.statement: Equation (\ref{bc1}) parametrises all self-adjoint extensions of the bulk Hamiltonian $-\prt_x^2$ to the whole graph and gives rise to non-trivial one-body interactions, which are described by the scattering matrix \cite{ks-00}-\cite{k-08}
nodes.statement_short: The vertex boundary condition exhausts the self-adjoint extensions of $-\prt_x^2$ on the star graph.
nodes.section: 2.1 Particle current in the presence of defect
conclusions: parametrises all self-adjoint extensions of the bulk Hamiltonian $-\prt_x^2$ to the whole graph
gives rise to non-trivial one-body interactions, which are described by the scattering matrix

nodes.name: Scattering matrix $\S(k)$ of the point-like defect
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \S(k) = -\frac{[\eta (\II - \UU) - k(\II+\UU )]}{[\eta (\II - \UU) + k(\II+\UU)]} \, , \end{equation} $k$ being the particle momentum.
nodes.statement_short: Vertex scattering matrix as a Möbius function of the momentum $k$ built from $\UU$ and $\eta$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Particle current in the presence of defect

nodes.name: Completeness of the class of point-like contact interactions
nodes.statement: We stress that the scattering matrices (\ref{S1}) provide a physical description of all point-like contact interactions among the leads, which are compatible with a unitary time evolution in the bulk of the system. This is the fundamental requirement selecting the class of defects considered in this paper.
nodes.statement_short: The family (\ref{S1}) covers every point-like defect compatible with unitary bulk evolution.
nodes.section: 2.1 Particle current in the presence of defect
assumptions: compatible with a unitary time evolution in the bulk of the system
conclusions: the scattering matrices (\ref{S1}) provide a physical description of all point-like contact interactions among the leads

nodes.name: Solution of the quantum boundary value problem
nodes.statement: The solution of (\ref{eqm1},\ref{bc1}) is given by \begin{equation} \psi (t,x,i) = \sum_{j=1}^N \int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{dk}{2\pi } \e^{-\ri \omega (k)t}\, \chi_{ij}(k;x) a_j (k) \, , \qquad \omega(k) = \frac {k^2}{2m} \, . \end{equation} where \begin{equation} \chi(k;x) = \e^{-\ri k x}\, \II + \e^{\ri k x}\, \S(-k) \end{equation} and $\{a_i(k),\, a^*_i(k)\, :\, k \geq 0,\, i=1,...,N\}$ generate the standard canonical anticommutation relation algebra.
nodes.statement_short: The field is a scattering-state expansion in $\chi(k;x)=\e^{-\ri kx}\II+\e^{\ri kx}\S(-k)$ over CAR generators.
nodes.section: 2.1 Particle current in the presence of defect

nodes.name: Particle current operator $j(t,x,i)$
nodes.statement: With the above definitions the particle current takes the form\footnote{The ${}^*$ stands for Hermitian conjugation.} \begin{eqnarray} j(t,x,i)= \frac{\ri}{2m} \int_0^\infty \frac{\rd k}{2\pi} \int_0^\infty \frac{\rd p}{2\pi}\, \e^{\ri t [\omega(k) - \omega(p)]} \qquad \qquad \qquad \nonumber \\ \times \sum_{l,m=1}^N a^*_l(k) \Bigl \{ \chi^*_{li}(k;x) \left [\der_{x} \chi_{i m}\right ](p;x) - \left [\der_{x} \chi^*_{li}\right ](k;x) \chi_{im}(p;x) \Bigr \}a_m(p) \, . \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Explicit bilinear form of the particle current operator in terms of the $\chi$ modes.
nodes.section: 2.1 Particle current in the presence of defect

nodes.name: Operator Kirchhoff rule
nodes.statement: Using the orthogonality and completeness of the system $\{\chi(k;x)\,:\, k\geq 0\, ,x\geq 0\}$ one can prove \cite{M-11} the operator Kirchhoff rule \begin{equation} \sum_{i=1}^N j(t,0,i) = 0\, , \end{equation} which is a simple but fundamental feature of the currents flowing in the junction.
nodes.statement_short: The currents entering the vertex sum to zero as an operator identity.
nodes.section: 2.1 Particle current in the presence of defect
assumptions: the orthogonality and completeness of the system $\{\chi(k;x)\,:\, k\geq 0\, ,x\geq 0\}$

nodes.name: Landauer-Büttiker non-equilibrium steady state $\Omega_{\beta,\mu}$
nodes.statement: The physical setting, presented in Fig. \ref{fig1}, is nicely described by the Landauer-B\"uttiker (LB) \cite{L-57, B-86} non-equilibrium steady state $\Omega_{\beta, \mu}$, defined in terms of $(\beta_i,\mu_i)$ and $\S(k)$. A simple and intuitive way \cite{M-11} to construct this state is to use the scattering matrix $\S(k)$ in order to extend the tensor product of Gibbs states, relative to the reservoirs $R_i$ at the level of asymptotic incoming fields, to the outgoing fields.
nodes.statement_short: The LB state extends the reservoirs' Gibbs states from incoming to outgoing fields via $\S(k)$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Particle current in the presence of defect
differentia: use the scattering matrix $\S(k)$ in order to extend the tensor product of Gibbs states, relative to the reservoirs $R_i$ at the level of asymptotic incoming fields, to the outgoing fields

nodes.name: $n$-point current correlation function $\W^i_n$
nodes.statement: Let $L_i$ be an arbitrary but fixed lead and let us consider the $n$-point correlation function \begin{equation} \W^i_n(t_1, x_1,...,t_n,x_n) = \langle j(t_1,x_1,i) \cdots j(t_n,x_n,i) \rangle_{\beta,\mu}\, , \end{equation} of the current (\ref{curr1}), where $\langle \cdots \rangle_{\beta,\mu}$ denotes the expectation value in the LB state $\Omega_{\beta, \mu}$.
nodes.statement_short: $\W^i_n$ is the $n$-fold current expectation value in the LB state on a fixed lead $L_i$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Current cumulants in the LB state
differentia: expectation value in the LB state $\Omega_{\beta, \mu}$

nodes.name: $n$-th current cumulant $\C^i_n$
nodes.statement: The $n$-th cumulant in $L_i$ is defined by the {\it connected} part of (\ref{w1}), \begin{equation} \C^i_n(t_1, x_1,...,t_n,x_n) = \langle j(t_1,x_1,i) \cdots j(t_n,x_n,i) \rangle_{\beta,\mu}^{\rm conn}\, . \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2.2 Current cumulants in the LB state

nodes.name: Fermi distribution $d_l(\omega)$ of the reservoir $R_l$
nodes.statement: d_l(\omega)= \frac{1}{1+\e^{\beta_l (\omega -\mu_l)}}
nodes.section: 2.2 Current cumulants in the LB state

nodes.name: Complementary distribution $\td_l(\omega)$
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \td_l(\omega ) = 1-d_l(\omega)=\frac{\e^{\beta_l (\omega -\mu_l)}}{1+\e^{\beta_l (\omega -\mu_l)}}\, . \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2.2 Current cumulants in the LB state

nodes.name: First cumulant in the LB state
nodes.statement: {}For $n=1$ the correlators (\ref{w1},\ref{c1}) coincide and have the following well known \cite{L-57, B-86} time and space independent form \begin{equation} \W^i_1 = \C^i_1 = \int_0^\infty \frac{\rd \omega}{2\pi} \sum_{l=1}^N \left (\delta_{il} -|\S_{il}(\sqrt{2m\omega})|^2\right ) d_l(\omega) \, , \qquad d_l(\omega)= \frac{1}{1+\e^{\beta_l (\omega -\mu_l)}}\, . \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The mean current is the Landauer-Büttiker energy integral over transmission-weighted Fermi factors.
nodes.section: 2.2 Current cumulants in the LB state

nodes.name: Time-difference and coordinate dependence for $n\geq 2$
nodes.statement: The situation complicates for $n\geq 2$. First of all the correlators (\ref{w1},\ref{c1}) depend on the time differences $\{\wt_k \equiv t_k - t_{k+1}\, :\, k=1,...,n-1\}$, which reflects the invariance under time translations of the LB state. Moreover, since the defect violates translation invariance in space, (\ref{w1},\ref{c1}) depend separately on all the coordinates $\{x_l\, :\, l=1,...,n\}$. It is clear that dealing with this large number of variables becomes complicated with growing of $n$. Also, it turns out that most of them are marginal for the particle transfer we are interested in.
nodes.statement_short: For $n\ge2$ the correlators depend on $n-1$ time differences and all $n$ coordinates, most of them marginal.
nodes.section: 2.2 Current cumulants in the LB state

nodes.name: Zero-frequency limit $\Z^i_n$
nodes.statement_short: Generalise zero-frequency noise to $n\ge3$ by Fourier transforming in the time differences and letting $\nu\to0^+$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Current cumulants in the LB state

nodes.name: Determinant form of the zero-frequency $\W^i_n$
nodes.statement: We will show below that in this limit the $x_l$-dependence drops out and $\Z^i_n$ depends exclusively on the scattering matrix $\S$ and the heat bath parameters $(\beta_l,\mu_l)$. In fact, using the explicit form of the current (\ref{curr1}) and the correlation function (\ref{A6}) in appendix A, after some algebra one finds \begin{eqnarray} \W^i_n=\int_0^\infty \frac{\rd \omega}{2\pi} \sum_{l_1,...,l_n=1}^N \left | \begin{array}{cccccccc} \T^i_{l_1l_1}(\omega)d_{l_1}(\omega )&\T^i_{l_2l_1}(\omega)d_{l_2}(\omega )&\cdots &&  \T^i_{l_nl_1}(\omega)d_{l_n}(\omega )\\ -\T^i_{l_1l_2}(\omega)\td_{l_1}(\omega )&\T^i_{l_2l_2}(\omega)d_{l_2}(\omega )& \cdots & &\T^i_{l_nl_2}(\omega)d_{l_n}(\omega )\\ \vdots &\vdots & \vdots&& \vdots \\ -\T^i_{l_1l_n}(\omega)\td_{l_1}(\omega )&-\T^i_{l_2l_n}(\omega)\td_{l_2}(\omega ) & \cdots & &\T^i_{l_nl_n}(\omega)d_{l_n}(\omega )\\ \end{array}\right | \, , \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: At zero frequency the $x_l$-dependence drops and $\W^i_n$ becomes an energy integral of an $n\times n$ determinant in $\T^i$, $d_l$, $\td_l$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Current cumulants in the LB state
assumptions: using the explicit form of the current (\ref{curr1}) and the correlation function (\ref{A6}) in appendix A
conclusions: in this limit the $x_l$-dependence drops out and $\Z^i_n$ depends exclusively on the scattering matrix $\S$ and the heat bath parameters $(\beta_l,\mu_l)$

nodes.name: $\T$-matrix $\T^i_{lm}(\omega)$
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \T^i_{lm}(\omega)=\delta_{li} \delta_{mi} - \S_{li}(\sqrt{2m\omega})\, \overline{\S}_{mi}(\sqrt{2m\omega})\, , \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2.2 Current cumulants in the LB state

nodes.name: Matrices $\mA^i$, $\mB^i$ and $\D$
nodes.statement: As expected, the connected part of (\ref{w2}) simplifies and can be conveniently written in terms of traces involving the matrices \begin{equation} \mA^i \equiv \T^i \, \D\, ,\qquad \mB^i \equiv \T^i\, (\II-\D)\, ,\qquad \D \equiv {\rm diag}[d_1(\omega),d_2(\omega),...,d_n(\omega)] \, . \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Auxiliary matrices $\mA^i=\T^i\D$ and $\mB^i=\T^i(\II-\D)$ with $\D$ the diagonal matrix of Fermi factors.
nodes.section: 2.2 Current cumulants in the LB state

nodes.name: Trace representation of the current cumulants
nodes.statement: One finds \begin{eqnarray} \C_1^i &=& \int_0^\infty \frac{\rd \omega}{2\pi} {\rm Tr} \left [ \mA^i \right ]\, , \\ \C_n^i &=& \int_0^\infty \frac{\rd \omega}{2\pi} \sum_{\sigma \in {\cal P}_{n-1}} \, {\rm Tr} \left [ \mA^i \mC^i_{\sigma_1\sigma_2}\cdots \mC^i_{\sigma_{n-2}\sigma_{n-1}}\mB^i\right ]\, , \qquad n \geq 2\, , \end{eqnarray} where the sum runs over all permutations ${\cal P}_{n-1}$ of $n-1$ elements and \begin{equation} \mC^i_{\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}} = \begin{cases} \, -\mA^i \, , & \qquad  \sigma_i < \sigma_{i+1}\, , \\ \quad \mB^i \, , & \qquad  \sigma_i > \sigma_{i+1}\, . \\ \end{cases} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Every zero-frequency cumulant is an energy integral of a sum over permutations of traces of alternating $\mA^i$/$\mB^i$ words.
nodes.section: 2.2 Current cumulants in the LB state
assumptions: the sum runs over all permutations ${\cal P}_{n-1}$ of $n-1$ elements

nodes.name: Purely field-theoretical derivation of $\C^i_n$
nodes.statement: The trace representation (\ref{c51},\ref{c52}) of the current cumulants with a point-like defect represents a first basic result of our study. It is worth stressing that the above derivation of $\C^i_n$ is purely field theoretical and makes no use of any kind of cumulant generating function. We will show in section 3 that this function can be uniquely reconstructed from (\ref{c51},\ref{c52}).
nodes.statement_short: The cumulants are obtained directly from field theory, with the generating function reconstructed only afterwards.
nodes.section: 2.2 Current cumulants in the LB state

nodes.name: The first six cumulants of the two-lead junction
nodes.statement: In order to better illustrate the compact expressions (\ref{c51},\ref{c52}), it is instructive report the explicit form of the first few cumulants in the case $N=2$. Without loss of generality we can concentrate on the the cumulants $\C_n^1$ in the lead $L_1$. For notational simplicity we omit here and in what follows the apex $1$ in $\C_n^1$. By means of (\ref{c51})-(\ref{m2}) one gets \begin{eqnarray} \C_1 &=& \int_0^\infty \frac{\rd \omega}{2\pi}\, \tau c_1\, , \\ \C_2 &=& \int_0^\infty \frac{\rd \omega}{2\pi}\, \tau (c_2 -\tau c_1^2)\, , \\ \C_3 &=& \int_0^\infty \frac{\rd \omega}{2\pi}\, \tau^2 c_1(1-3c_2+2\tau c_1^2) \, , \\ \C_4 &=& \int_0^\infty \frac{\rd \omega}{2\pi}\, \tau^2[c_2 -3c_2^2+12\tau c_1^2c_2 - 2\tau c_1^2(2+3\tau c_1^2)]\, , \\ \C_5 &=& \int_0^\infty \frac{\rd \omega}{2\pi}\, \tau^3 c_1[1+30c_2^2 -15c_2(1+4\tau c_1^2) + 4\tau c_1^2(5+6\tau c_1^2)]\, , \\ \C_6 &=& \int_0^\infty \frac{\rd \omega}{2\pi}\, \tau^3 \{c_2[1+15c_2(2c_2-1)] - 2\tau c_1^2[8+15c_2(9c_2-5)] + \nonumber \\ &+&120 \tau^2 c_1^4(3c_2-1) -120\tau^3 c_1^6\}\, , \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Explicit $N=2$ cumulants $\C_1,\dots,\C_6$ as energy integrals of polynomials in $\tau$, $c_1$, $c_2$.

nodes.name: Distribution combinations $c_1(\omega)$ and $c_2(\omega)$
nodes.statement: where the following combinations \begin{equation} c_1(\omega)\equiv d_1(\omega)-d_2(\omega)\, \qquad c_2(\omega)\equiv d_1(\omega)+d_2(\omega)-2d_1(\omega)d_2(\omega)\, , \end{equation} have been introduced for convenience.

nodes.name: Transmission probability $\tau(\omega)$ of the two-lead junction
nodes.statement: Moreover, the transmission probability associated with the $\S$-matrix (\ref{S1}) is given by \begin{equation} \tau(\omega) = |\S_{12}(\sqrt{2m\omega})|^2 = \frac{2m\omega (\eta_1-\eta_2)^2 \sin^2 (\theta)}{(2m\omega+\eta_1^2)(2m\omega+\eta_2^2)} \, , \qquad \theta \in [0,2\pi)\, , \end{equation} with \begin{equation} \eta_i \equiv \eta\, {\rm tan} (\alpha_i)\, , \qquad  \alpha_i \in [-\pi/2, \pi/2)\, , \end{equation} $\left (e^{-2i\alpha_1}, e^{-2i\alpha_2} \right )$ being the eigenvalues of the matrix $\UU$ entering the boundary condition (\ref{bc1}).
nodes.statement_short: $\tau(\omega)=|\S_{12}|^2$ expressed through the mass scales $\eta_i=\eta\tan\alpha_i$ fixed by the eigenvalues of $\UU$.

nodes.name: Ansatz for the cumulant generating function
nodes.statement: Following the pioneering work of Khlus \cite{K-87}, Lesovik and Levitov \cite{L-89, LL-92}, we look for a generating function in the form \begin{equation} \C (\lambda ) = \int_0^\infty \frac{\rd \omega}{2\pi}\, \ln \left [1+F_{12}(\tau,d_1,d_2)\left (\e^{\ri \lambda f(\tau)}-1\right ) + F_{21}(\tau,d_1,d_2)\left (\e^{-\ri \lambda f(\tau)}-1\right )\right ] \, , \end{equation} where $F_{12}$, $F_{21}$ and $f$ are unknown functions.
nodes.statement_short: Logarithmic Levitov-Lesovik ansatz for $\C(\lambda)$ with three unknown functions $F_{12},F_{21},f$.

nodes.name: Standard definition of the cumulant generating function
nodes.statement: Using the standard definition of generating function \begin{equation} \C_n = (-\ri \partial_\lambda)^n\, \C(\lambda ) \vert_{{}_{\lambda =0}} \end{equation}

nodes.name: Determination of $F_{12}$, $F_{21}$ and $f$
nodes.statement: and the information from the first three cumulants $\C_1$, $\C_2$ and $\C_3$ only, one can easily determine $F_{12}$, $F_{21}$ and $f$. The simple result \begin{equation} F_{12} = \frac{1}{2}(c_2 + c_1\sqrt{\tau})\, , \qquad F_{21} = \frac{1}{2}(c_2 - c_1\sqrt{\tau})\, , \qquad f=\sqrt{\tau}\, . \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The three unknown functions are fixed by $\C_1,\C_2,\C_3$ to $F_{12,21}=\tfrac12(c_2\pm c_1\sqrt\tau)$ and $f=\sqrt\tau$.
assumptions: the information from the first three cumulants $\C_1$, $\C_2$ and $\C_3$ only

nodes.name: Cumulant generating function of the two-lead junction
nodes.statement: leads to the following generating function \begin{eqnarray} \C (\lambda ) &=& \int_0^\infty \frac{\rd \omega}{2\pi}\, \ln \left [1+\frac{1}{2}(c_2+c_1\sqrt{\tau})\left (\e^{\ri \lambda \sqrt{\tau}}-1\right ) + \frac{1}{2}(c_2-c_1\sqrt{\tau})\left (\e^{-\ri \lambda \sqrt{\tau}}-1\right )\right ] \nonumber \\ &=&\int_0^\infty \frac{\rd \omega}{2\pi}\, \ln \left \{1+ \ri c_1 \sqrt{\tau}\, \sin (\lambda  \sqrt{\tau}) +c_2 \left [\cos (\lambda  \sqrt{\tau})-1\right ] \right \} \, . \end{eqnarray} One can easily check also that (\ref{gf4}) reproduces perfectly the cumulants $\C_4$, $\C_5$ and $\C_6$ as well and represents therefore a valid candidate for the final result in the case of two leads.
nodes.statement_short: Closed logarithmic generating function for $N=2$, verified against $\C_4,\C_5,\C_6$.
conclusions: (\ref{gf4}) reproduces perfectly the cumulants $\C_4$, $\C_5$ and $\C_6$ as well

nodes.name: Statistical independence of the energy channels
nodes.statement: The argument in what follows is based on the fact that the particle transport in our system can be separated in statistically independent processes with fixed energy. In fact, excitations with different energies propagate in the graph in Fig. \ref{fig1} in a fully independent way, because the only interaction, localised in the vertex, leaves the energy invariant (see (\ref{A7})).
nodes.statement_short: Transport factorises over energy channels because the vertex interaction conserves energy.
assumptions: the only interaction, localised in the vertex, leaves the energy invariant
conclusions: the particle transport in our system can be separated in statistically independent processes with fixed energy

nodes.name: Additivity of the cumulants over energy channels
nodes.statement: For this reason one can focus first on a single energy channel $\omega$, thus dealing with a system with finite degrees of freedom. This fact significantly simplifies the problem and allows to derive explicitly the single energy channel cumulant generating function $\C_\omega^i(\lambda )$ in the lead $L_i$. The final step is to integrate over all energies, \begin{equation} \C^i(\lambda ) = \int_0^\infty \frac{\rd \omega}{2\pi}\, \C_\omega^i(\lambda )\, , \end{equation} using at this stage the well known property that the total cumulant of a process, which can be decomposed in statistically independent subprocesses, is the sum of the cumulants of each of the latter.
nodes.statement_short: The total generating function is the energy integral of the single-channel one, by additivity of cumulants over independent subprocesses.
assumptions: a process, which can be decomposed in statistically independent subprocesses
conclusions: the total cumulant of a process ... is the sum of the cumulants of each of the latter

nodes.name: Single energy channel particle current $j_\omega^i$
nodes.statement: In order to obtain the particle current of a single energy channel $\omega\geq 0$, we modify the integration measure in the general expression of the particle current (\ref{curr1}) according to \begin{equation} \rd k\, \rd p \longmapsto \rd k\, \rd p\, (2\pi)^2\, \delta \left (\frac{k^2}{2m} - \omega \right ) \delta (k-p)\, , \end{equation} which selects the contribution with energy $\omega$. This operation leads to the simple time and position independent expression \begin{equation} j_\omega^i = \sum_{l,m=1}^N a^*_l\, \T^i_{lm}(\sqrt{2m\omega})\, a_m \, , \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Restricting the current measure to energy $\omega$ gives the time- and position-independent bilinear $j_\omega^i=a^*_l\T^i_{lm}a_m$.

nodes.name: Standard fermionic oscillators
nodes.statement: where $\{a_i, a_i^*\}$ are standard fermionic oscillators: \begin{equation} [a_i\, ,\, a_j^*]_+ = \delta_{ij}\, ,\qquad [a_i\, ,\, a_j]_+ = [a^*_i\, ,\, a_j^*]_+ = 0\, , \qquad \langle a^*_i a_j\rangle_{\beta,\mu} = \delta_{ij} d_j(\omega)\, . \end{equation}

nodes.name: Single-channel cumulant generating function $\C_\omega^i(\lambda)$
nodes.statement: Now, the generating function of cumulants in the channel $\omega$ and lead $L_i$ is given by \begin{equation} \C_\omega^i(\lambda ) = \ln \langle \e^{\ri \lambda j_w^i} \rangle_{\beta,\mu} \, . \end{equation}

nodes.name: Determinant formula for $\langle \e^{\ri \lambda j_w^i}\rangle_{\beta,\mu}$
nodes.statement: The expectation value $\langle \e^{\ri \lambda j_w^i} \rangle_{\beta,\mu}$ can be evaluated explicitly. The key points of the computation, which leads to the final result \begin{equation} \langle \e^{\ri \lambda j_w^i} \rangle_{\beta,\mu} = {\rm det} \left [\II + \left (\e^{\ri \lambda \T^i(\sqrt{2m\omega})} -\II \right ) \D(\omega) \right ]\, ,   \qquad   \D(\omega ) \equiv {\rm diag}[d_1(\omega),d_2(\omega),...,d_n(\omega)] \, , \end{equation} are given appendix C.
nodes.statement_short: The single-channel characteristic function is a Fredholm-type determinant in $\e^{\ri\lambda\T^i}-\II$ and $\D$.

nodes.name: Total transmission probability $\tau(\omega)$ for $N$ terminals
nodes.statement: Here \begin{equation} \tau(\omega) = \sum_{i=2}^N \tau_i (\omega)\, , \qquad  \tau_i (\omega) \equiv |\S_{1i}(\sqrt{2m\omega})|^2 \, , \end{equation} is the total transmission probability between the lead $L_1$ and the remaining $N-1$ leads $L_i$
differentia: between the lead $L_1$ and the remaining $N-1$ leads $L_i$

nodes.name: Effective Fermi distribution $d_2^{\rm eff}$
nodes.statement: and $c_{1,2}^{\rm eff}$ are obtained from (\ref{dc}) by the substitution \begin{equation} d_2 (\omega) \longrightarrow d_2^{\rm eff} (\omega) \equiv \sum_{i=2}^N\frac{ \tau_i (\omega)}{\tau(\omega)}\, d_i(\omega) \, , \end{equation} which represents an effective distribution where $d_i(\omega)$ with $i\geq 2$ are weighted by the ratios $\tau_i(\omega)/\tau(\omega)\in [0,1]$.
nodes.statement_short: All downstream reservoirs are lumped into one effective Fermi distribution weighted by transmission ratios.
differentia: where $d_i(\omega)$ with $i\geq 2$ are weighted by the ratios $\tau_i(\omega)/\tau(\omega)\in [0,1]$

nodes.name: Cumulant generating function for $N$ terminals
nodes.statement: In the lead $L_1$ one finds \begin{equation} \C(\lambda ) = \int_0^\infty \frac{\rd \omega}{2\pi}\, \ln \left \{1+ \ri c_1^{\rm eff} \sqrt{\tau}\, \sin \left (\lambda  \sqrt{\tau}\right ) +c_2^{\rm eff} \left [\cos \left (\lambda  \sqrt{\tau}\right )-1\right ] \right \} \, . \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The $N$-terminal generating function has the two-lead form with $c_{1,2}$ replaced by their effective counterparts.

nodes.name: Novelty of the multi-terminal generating function
nodes.statement: As expected, the expression (\ref{gf6}) reproduces (\ref{gf4}) for $N=2$. Summarising, we derived in explicit form the generating function of the cumulants (\ref{c51}, \ref{c52}) for the Schr\"odinger junction with $N>2$ leads. The novelty with respect to the two terminal case (\ref{gf4}) is the effective Fermi distribution (\ref{gf8}), which captures the presence of all $N-1>1$ reservoirs.
nodes.statement_short: The multi-terminal result reduces to $N=2$ and its only new ingredient is the effective Fermi distribution.

nodes.name: Classification of the scale invariant $\S$-matrices
nodes.statement: The scale invariant (critical) elements in the family (\ref{S1}) are fully classified \cite{Calabrese:2011ru} and belong to the orbits \begin{equation} \{{\cal U}\, \S_d\, {\cal U}^* \; :\; {\cal U} \in U(N),\; \S_d = {\rm diag}(\pm 1,\, \pm 1,\, ...\, ,\, \pm 1)\} \end{equation} of the adjoint action of the unitary group $U(N)$ on the diagonal matrices $\S_d$.
nodes.statement_short: Critical $\S$-matrices are exactly the $U(N)$ adjoint orbits of diagonal sign matrices.
assumptions: The scale invariant (critical) elements in the family (\ref{S1})
conclusions: belong to the orbits $\{{\cal U}\, \S_d\, {\cal U}^* \; :\; {\cal U} \in U(N),\; \S_d = {\rm diag}(\pm 1,\, \pm 1,\, ...\, ,\, \pm 1)\}$ of the adjoint action of the unitary group $U(N)$ on the diagonal matrices $\S_d$

nodes.name: Variables $\gamma_j$ and $\Lambda(\lambda)$
nodes.statement: In fact, introducing the variables \begin{equation} \gamma_j\equiv\e^{-\beta\mu_j}\, ,\qquad \Lambda(\lambda ) \equiv \ri \sqrt{\tau}(\gamma_2-\gamma_1)\sin(\lambda\sqrt{\tau}) +(\gamma_2+\gamma_1)\cos(\lambda\sqrt{\tau})\, , \end{equation} where $\tau=|\S_{12}|^2$ now is constant,

nodes.name: Cumulant generating function in the scale invariant limit
nodes.statement: one gets in the case $N=2$ \begin{equation} \begin{split} \C(\lambda) = \frac{1}{2\pi \beta}\Bigg\{ &\Li_2\left (-\gamma_1^{-1}\right ) + \Li_2\left (-\gamma_2^{-1}\right ) \\ -&\Li_2\left[\frac{-2}{\Lambda(\lambda) - \sqrt{\Lambda^2(\lambda)-4\gamma_1\gamma_2}}\right] - \Li_2\left[\frac{-2}{\Lambda(\lambda) + \sqrt{\Lambda^2(\lambda)-4\gamma_1\gamma_2}}\right] \Bigg\}\, , \end{split} \end{equation} $\Li_2$ being the dilogarithm function.
nodes.statement_short: For critical $\S$ and equal temperatures the energy integral is done in closed form by four dilogarithms.

nodes.name: Chemical potential variables $\mu_\pm$
nodes.statement: The results of \cite{MSS-15} suggest to investigate (\ref{si3}) as a function of \begin{equation} \mu_\pm = (\mu_1 \pm \mu_2)/2 \, , \end{equation} $\mu_+ \in \RR$ playing the role of control parameter.

nodes.name: Low temperature limit of $\C(\lambda)$ at $\mu_+=0$
nodes.statement: For $\mu_+=0$ the expression (\ref{si3}) greatly simplifies in the low temperature limit $\beta \to \infty$. In fact, one finds \begin{equation} \lim_{\beta \to \infty} \C (\lambda )\vert_{{}_{\mu_+=0}}  = \frac{|\mu_-|}{2\pi} \ln \left [\cos (\lambda \sqrt{\tau}) + \ri\, \varepsilon (\mu_-)\sqrt{\tau} \sin (\lambda \sqrt{\tau})\right ] \, , \end{equation} $\varepsilon$ being the sign function.
nodes.statement_short: At $\mu_+=0$ and $\beta\to\infty$ the dilogarithms collapse to a single logarithm proportional to $|\mu_-|$.

nodes.name: Independent derivation by Levitov and Lesovik as a check
nodes.statement: The result (\ref{si4}) was derived for $\mu_->0$ independently by Levitov and Lesovik \cite{LL-92, LS-14} and provides therefore a valuable check on (\ref{si3}).

nodes.name: First four cumulants in the scale invariant low temperature limit
nodes.statement: For the first few cumulants one gets from (\ref{si4}) \begin{equation} \C_1 = \frac{\tau \mu_-}{2\pi} \, ,\qquad \C_2 = \frac{\tau (1-\tau)|\mu_-|}{2\pi}\, ,\qquad \C_3 = \frac{\tau^2(\tau-1) \mu_-}{\pi}\, ,\qquad \C_4 = \frac{ \tau^2(\tau-1)(1-3\tau) |\mu_-|}{\pi}\, . \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Explicit $\C_1$–$\C_4$ linear in $\mu_-$ (or $|\mu_-|$) with polynomial $\tau$ prefactors.

nodes.name: Proportionality of odd cumulants to the current
nodes.statement: From (\ref{si4}) one infers that for any $n\geq 0$ \begin{equation} \C_{2n+1}\propto \C_1\, , \qquad \mu_+=0\, , \quad \beta \to \infty\, , \end{equation} which provides an interesting signature for experiments.
nodes.statement_short: All odd cumulants are proportional to the mean current at $\mu_+=0$, $\beta\to\infty$.

nodes.name: Experimental evidence for the linear dependence of $\C_3$ on $\C_1$
nodes.statement: In fact, experimental evidence for the linear dependence of $\C_3$ on the current $\C_1$ in this regime has been reported in \cite{BGSLR-05}.

nodes.name: Transferred charge and the effective charge $e_{\rm eff}$
nodes.statement: It is instructive to derive the charge transferred through the junction in the time interval $[0,T]$. Since the LB state is stationary, one has in general \begin{equation} Q_T = \int_0^T \rd t\, \langle j(t,x,i)\rangle_{\beta,\mu} = T \C_1\, . \end{equation} Restoring the electric charge according to $j\longmapsto e j$ and $\mu_-=eV$, where $V$ is the applied voltage, one gets from (\ref{si5}) \begin{equation} Q_T = \frac{ e^2\tau}{2\pi} VT = \frac{ e_{\rm eff}^2}{2\pi} VT\, ,  \qquad e_{\rm eff}\equiv e \sqrt {\tau}\, , \end{equation} where the effective charge $e_{\rm eff}$ has been introduced.
nodes.statement_short: Stationarity gives $Q_T=T\C_1$, which in physical units defines the effective charge $e_{\rm eff}=e\sqrt\tau$.
assumptions: Since the LB state is stationary
Restoring the electric charge according to $j\longmapsto e j$ and $\mu_-=eV$, where $V$ is the applied voltage
conclusions: $Q_T = \frac{ e^2\tau}{2\pi} VT = \frac{ e_{\rm eff}^2}{2\pi} VT\, ,  \qquad e_{\rm eff}\equiv e \sqrt {\tau}$

nodes.name: Charge renormalisation induced by the defect
nodes.statement: We see that switching on the defect ($\tau < 1$) causes a finite renormalisation of the charge $e \longmapsto e_{\rm eff}$ with respect to the case in which the defect is absent ($\tau=1$). This purely quantum phenomenon is induced by the non-trivial reflection probability $(1-\tau)$ from the defect. In this respect the appearance of the effective charge $e_{\rm eff}$ in the probability distribution (\ref{Mo7}), reconstructed in section 4 below, is not surprising. It is worth mentioning that the same charge renormalisation effect has been observed in \cite{LL-92, LC-03} as well.
nodes.statement_short: A defect with $\tau<1$ renormalises the charge to $e\sqrt\tau$, a purely quantum reflection effect.

nodes.name: Nonlinear form of the current for $\mu_+\neq 0$
nodes.statement: Relevant non-linear effects show up \cite{MSS-15} for $\mu_+\not=0$. Consider for instance the current, which can be written in the form \begin{equation} \C_1=  \frac{\tau \mu_-}{2\pi}  + \frac{\tau}{2\pi \beta} \ln \left [\frac{\e^{\beta \mup}+\e^{-\beta \mum}}{1+\e^{\beta(\mup-\mum)}}\right ] \, . \end{equation} The second term vanishes for $\mu_+=0$, but is nontrivial otherwise and captures the nonlinear behavior close to the origin $\mu_-=0$, shown in the left panel of Fig. \ref{fig2}.
nodes.statement_short: The current splits into a linear term plus a logarithmic term that vanishes only at $\mu_+=0$.
conclusions: The second term vanishes for $\mu_+=0$, but is nontrivial otherwise

nodes.name: Asymptotic slopes of $\C_3$ and $\C_4$
nodes.statement: It follows from (\ref{si3}) that for $\mu_+\not=0$ the cumulants $\C_3$ and $\C_4$ are respectively odd and even nonlinear functions of $\mu_-$. For the slopes of the asymptotes at $\mu_-=\pm \infty$ one finds \begin{equation} \lim_{\mu_-\to \pm \infty} \frac{\C_3}{\mu_-} = \frac{\tau^2(\tau-1)}{\pi}\, ,\qquad \lim_{\mu_-\to \pm \infty} \frac{\C_4}{\mu_-} = \pm \frac{ \tau^2(\tau-1)(1-3\tau)}{\pi}\, , \end{equation} which depend on $\tau$ but not on $\beta$ and $\mu_+$.
nodes.statement_short: The large-$|\mu_-|$ slopes of $\C_3,\C_4$ depend only on $\tau$, not on $\beta$ or $\mu_+$.
conclusions: the cumulants $\C_3$ and $\C_4$ are respectively odd and even nonlinear functions of $\mu_-$

nodes.name: Minimal coupling of the LLL setup
nodes.statement: First of all, instead of the boundary condition (\ref{bc1}), which fixes the self-adjoint extension of the operator $-\partial_x^2$ in our framework, these authors introduced in (\ref{eqm1}) a minimal coupling \begin{equation} \ri \partial_x \longrightarrow \ri \partial_x + A(x)\, . \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: LLL replace the vertex boundary condition by minimal coupling to a classical potential $A(x)$.

nodes.name: Levitov-Lee-Lesovik generating function
nodes.statement: In the special case \begin{equation} A(x) \sim \lambda\, \delta(x) \end{equation} with a coupling proportional to the counting parameter $\lambda$, LLL got for sufficiently large $T$ \cite{LLL-96} (see also \cite{Sch-07}, \cite{LS-14} and the contributions to \cite{N-03}) \begin{eqnarray} \C_{L} (\lambda ) &=& \int_0^\infty \frac{\rd \omega}{2\pi}\, \ln \left [1+\frac{1}{2}(c_2+\tau c_1)\left (\e^{\ri \lambda}-1\right ) + \frac{1}{2}(c_2-\tau c_1)\left (\e^{-\ri \lambda}-1\right )\right ] \nonumber \\ &=&\int_0^\infty \frac{\rd \omega}{2\pi}\, \ln \left \{1+ \ri c_1 \tau\, \sin (\lambda) + \tau c_2 \left [\cos (\lambda ) -1\right ]\right \} \, . \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: For a delta-localised counting field LLL obtain a generating function with $\tau$ in place of $\sqrt\tau$.
assumptions: with a coupling proportional to the counting parameter $\lambda$

nodes.name: Agreement of the two schemes for the first two cumulants
nodes.statement: Nevertheless, comparing (\ref{gf4}) and (\ref{LL1}), we observe that these results coincide when the defect in the junction disconnects the leads ($\tau=0$), or when the defect is absent ($\tau=1$). Moreover, quite remarkably the first two cumulants generated by (\ref{gf4}) and (\ref{LL1}) coincide for any $\tau$. Therefore the transferred charge (\ref{si6},\ref{si7}) and the zero frequency quantum noise power $\C_2$ coincide in both schemes. For distinguishing the two settings, one should concentrate on the higher cumulants $\C_{n\geq 3}$. It turns out that they have the same monomials in $c_1$ and $c_2$, but with different powers of $\tau$.
nodes.statement_short: The two settings share $\C_1$ and $\C_2$ for every $\tau$ and differ only in the powers of $\tau$ from $\C_3$ on.
conclusions: these results coincide when the defect in the junction disconnects the leads ($\tau=0$), or when the defect is absent ($\tau=1$)
the first two cumulants generated by (\ref{gf4}) and (\ref{LL1}) coincide for any $\tau$
the transferred charge (\ref{si6},\ref{si7}) and the zero frequency quantum noise power $\C_2$ coincide in both schemes
they have the same monomials in $c_1$ and $c_2$, but with different powers of $\tau$

nodes.name: Third and fourth LLL cumulants
nodes.statement: One has for instance \begin{eqnarray} \C_{L, 3} &=& \int_0^\infty \frac{\rd \omega}{2\pi}\, \tau c_1(1-3\tau c_2+2\tau c_1^2) \, , \\\ \C_{L, 4} &=& \int_0^\infty \frac{\rd \omega}{2\pi}\, \tau[c_2 -3\tau c_2^2+12\tau^2 c_1^2c_2 - 2\tau c_1^2(2+3\tau^2 c_1^2)]\, , \end{eqnarray} to be compared with (\ref{ec3},\ref{ec4}).
nodes.statement_short: Explicit $\C_{L,3}$ and $\C_{L,4}$ for comparison with the paper's $\C_3,\C_4$.

nodes.name: Freedom in the choice of the external potential $A(x)$
nodes.statement: It is natural to expect that the form (\ref{LL1}) of $\C_L$ depends on the specific choice (\ref{minc2}) of the external potential, which implements the effective description of the charge detector. It has been argued in \cite{NK-03} that localising $A(x)$ at $x=0$ minimises the disturbance of the system due to the measuring device. The localisation of $A(x)$ in one point can be achieved however in many different ways, using general linear combinations of the delta function and its derivatives. The study of the freedom associated with $A(x)$ is beyond the scope of the present paper, which is focussed on the properties of the cumulants (\ref{c51},\ref{c52}), uniquely defined by the connected current correlation functions (\ref{c1}) in the quantum boundary value problem (\ref{eqm1},\ref{bc1}).
nodes.statement_short: The LLL result depends on the choice of $A(x)$; exploring that freedom is left aside.

nodes.name: Moment generating function at fixed energy $\chi_\omega(\lambda)$
nodes.statement: In our case the moment generating function at fixed energy $\omega$ for the two-lead junction can be extracted from equation (\ref{C4}) in appendix C. One has \begin{equation} \chi_\omega (\lambda) = 1+ \ri c_1\sqrt{\tau}\, \sin \left (\lambda \sqrt{\tau }\right )+ c_2 \left [\cos \left (\lambda \sqrt{\tau} \right )-1\right ]\, , \end{equation} where $c_i(\omega)$ and $\tau(\omega)$ are given by (\ref{dc}-\ref{tr1}).
nodes.statement_short: The fixed-energy moment generating function is the argument of the logarithm in the two-lead $\C(\lambda)$.
assumptions: at fixed energy $\omega$ for the two-lead junction

nodes.name: Moments $m_n$
nodes.statement: The moments $\{m_n\, :\, n=0,1,...\}$ are inferred from the expansion \begin{equation} \chi_\omega (\lambda) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(\ri \lambda)^n}{n!}\, m_n \end{equation}

nodes.name: Closed form of the moments $m_n$
nodes.statement: and have the simple general form \begin{equation} m_n  = \begin{cases} \,1 \, , & n=0\, , \\ c_1 \tau^{k}\, , & n=2k-1\, ,\quad \; k=1,2,...\, , \\ c_2 \tau^{k}\, , & n=2k\, ,\quad \qquad k=1,2,...\, . \\ \end{cases} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Odd moments are $c_1\tau^k$, even ones $c_2\tau^k$ — far simpler than the cumulants.

nodes.name: Moments are simpler than cumulants
nodes.statement: One can verify that (\ref{Mo2}) and the cumulants at energy $\omega$, given by the integrands of (\ref{c51}, \ref{c52}) (see also (\ref{ec1}-\ref{ec6})), satisfy the conventional relations between moments and cumulants. The nice surprise is that for generic $n$ the moment $m_n$ is much simpler then the corresponding cumulant.
nodes.statement_short: Moments and cumulants satisfy the usual relations, yet $m_n$ is much simpler than $\C_n$.

nodes.name: The moment problem
nodes.statement: This fact represents a great technical advantage for solving the moment problem, namely for determining a probability distribution $\varphi (\xi)$ such that \begin{equation} m_n = \int_{\cal D} \rd \xi\, \xi^n \varphi (\xi)\, . \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Find $\varphi(\xi)$ on a domain $\cal D$ whose $n$-th moment is $m_n$.

nodes.name: Hankel determinant criterion for the moment problem
nodes.statement: There exist \cite{ST-70} three possible choices for the domain $\cal D$: the whole line ${\cal D}=\RR$, the half line ${\cal D}= \RR_+$ and a compact interval ${\cal D}=[a,b]$. A necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of $\varphi$ on $\RR$ is \cite{ST-70} the non-negativity of the Hankel determinants \begin{equation} \HH_n \equiv \left | \begin{array}{cccccccc} m_0&m_1&\cdots &&  m_n\\ m_1&m_2& \cdots & &m_{n+1}\\ \vdots &\vdots & \vdots&& \vdots \\ m_n&m_{n+1}& \cdots & &m_{2n}\\ \end{array}\right | \geq 0\, . \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Existence of $\varphi$ on $\RR$ is equivalent to non-negativity of all Hankel determinants of the moments.
assumptions: three possible choices for the domain $\cal D$: the whole line ${\cal D}=\RR$, the half line ${\cal D}= \RR_+$ and a compact interval ${\cal D}=[a,b]$
conclusions: A necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of $\varphi$ on $\RR$ is the non-negativity of the Hankel determinants $\HH_n \geq 0$

nodes.name: Hankel determinants of the junction and existence of $\varphi$
nodes.statement: {}From (\ref{Mo3}) one gets \begin{equation} \HH_0 = 1\, , \qquad \HH_1=\tau(c_2-c^2_1\tau)\, , \qquad \HH_2=\tau^3(1-c_2)(c_2^2-c_1^2\tau)\, , \qquad \HH_{n\geq 3} = 0\, . \end{equation} Using the explicit form of $c_i$ and that $\tau \in [0,1]$, one can show that $\HH_2$ and $\HH_3$ are non-negative. Therefore the probability distribution $\varphi$ on $\RR$ exists.
nodes.statement_short: Only $\HH_0,\HH_1,\HH_2$ are nonzero and they are non-negative, so $\varphi$ exists on $\RR$.
assumptions: Using the explicit form of $c_i$ and that $\tau \in [0,1]$
conclusions: Therefore the probability distribution $\varphi$ on $\RR$ exists

nodes.name: Reduction to the Hamburger moment problem
nodes.statement: Combining the results of \cite{ST-70} with \begin{equation} \HH_2^\prime \equiv \left | \begin{array}{cccccccc} m_1&m_2\\ m_2&m_3\\ \end{array}\right | = \tau^2 (c_1\tau -c_2) \leq 0\, , \end{equation} one concludes that the domains $\RR_+$ and $[a,b]$ are excluded and one il left therefore with the so called Hamburger moment problem ${\cal D}=\RR$.
nodes.statement_short: A negative shifted Hankel determinant rules out $\RR_+$ and $[a,b]$, leaving the Hamburger problem on $\RR$.
conclusions: one il left therefore with the so called Hamburger moment problem ${\cal D}=\RR$

nodes.name: Probability distribution $\varphi(\xi)$ of the two-lead junction
nodes.statement: Moreover, since $\HH_{n\geq 3} = 0$ the general theory \cite{ST-70} implies that $\varphi$ is localised in three different points on the $\xi$-line. In fact, employing (\ref{Mo0}-\ref{Mo3}), one finds \begin{equation} \begin{split} \varphi (\xi) &= \int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac{\rd \lambda}{2\pi}\, \e^{-\ri \lambda \xi}\, \chi_\omega (\lambda ) \\ &=\frac{1}{2}(c_2-c_1\sqrt {\tau})\delta(\xi +e\sqrt {\tau})+(1-c_2) \delta(\xi) + \frac{1}{2}(c_2+c_1\sqrt {\tau})\delta(\xi -e \sqrt {\tau}) \, , \end{split} \end{equation} where the charge $e$ has been restored for clarifying the physical interpretation of $\varphi$.
nodes.statement_short: The reconstructed distribution is a sum of three delta functions supported at $-e\sqrt\tau$, $0$ and $e\sqrt\tau$.
conclusions: $\varphi$ is localised in three different points on the $\xi$-line

nodes.name: Emission-absorption probabilities $p_{ij}$
nodes.statement: The basic microscopic process, which takes place in the system for $\tau\not=0$, is the emission of a particle with energy $\omega$ from a reservoir $R_i$ and its absorption from $R_j$. Let us denote by $p_{ij}$ the relative probability. Recalling that $\varphi$ concerns the lead $L_1$, the three terms in (\ref{Mo7}) correspond to the three elementary processes of emission and absorption relative to the reservoir $R_1$, namely: (i) $p_{12}=\frac{1}{2}(c_2-c_1\sqrt {\tau})$ is the probability for a particle to be emitted from $R_1$ and absorbed by $R_2$; (ii) $p_{11}=(1-c_2)$ is the probability for a particle to be emitted from and absorbed by $R_1$; (iii) $p_{21}=\frac{1}{2}(c_2+c_1\sqrt {\tau})$ is the probability for a particle to be emitted from $R_2$ and absorbed by $R_1$.
nodes.statement_short: The three weights of $\varphi$ are the probabilities $p_{12}$, $p_{11}$, $p_{21}$ of the elementary emission-absorption processes.
differentia: the emission of a particle with energy $\omega$ from a reservoir $R_i$ and its absorption from $R_j$
$p_{12}=\frac{1}{2}(c_2-c_1\sqrt {\tau})$ is the probability for a particle to be emitted from $R_1$ and absorbed by $R_2$
$p_{11}=(1-c_2)$ is the probability for a particle to be emitted from and absorbed by $R_1$
$p_{21}=\frac{1}{2}(c_2+c_1\sqrt {\tau})$ is the probability for a particle to be emitted from $R_2$ and absorbed by $R_1$

nodes.name: Charge variation supported at $0$ and $\pm e_{\rm eff}$
nodes.statement: The variation $\xi$ of the charge in $L_1$, involved in these processes, is fixed by the support of the delta functions in (\ref{Mo7}) and is $\xi = e_{\rm eff}$, $\xi=0$ and $\xi=- e_{\rm eff}$ respectively, $e_{\rm eff}$ being defined in (\ref{si7}). These values of $\xi$ are consistent with the physical interpretation of (i)-(iii). It is worth stressing that $p_{11}$ is $\tau$-independent as intuitively expected.
nodes.statement_short: The transferred charge takes only the values $\pm e_{\rm eff}$ and $0$, and $p_{11}$ is $\tau$-independent.
assumptions: fixed by the support of the delta functions in (\ref{Mo7})
conclusions: The variation $\xi$ of the charge in $L_1$ ... is $\xi = e_{\rm eff}$, $\xi=0$ and $\xi=- e_{\rm eff}$ respectively

nodes.name: Collapse of $\varphi$ for disconnected leads
nodes.statement: For $\tau=0$ the two leads are disconnected and one expects therefore that $p_{12} = p_{21}=0$ and $p_{11} =1$. This simple physical observation is confirmed by the fact that the three terms in (\ref{Mo7}) collapse in one, namely \begin{equation} \varphi (\xi)\vert_{\tau=0} = \delta(\xi)\, . \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: At $\tau=0$ the distribution reduces to $\delta(\xi)$, i.e. $p_{11}=1$ and $p_{12}=p_{21}=0$.
assumptions: For $\tau=0$ the two leads are disconnected

nodes.name: Discontinuity of the probabilities at $\tau=0$
nodes.statement: The property (\ref{Mo7b}) implies also that as functions of $\tau$ the probabilities $p_{ij}$ are discontinuous at $\tau=0$, when the system divides in two parts.
conclusions: as functions of $\tau$ the probabilities $p_{ij}$ are discontinuous at $\tau=0$, when the system divides in two parts

nodes.name: Distribution in the second lead and $p_{22}=p_{11}$
nodes.statement: The probability distribution $\varphi$ in $L_2$ is obtained by implementing $d_1 \leftrightarrow d_2$, or equivalently (see (\ref{dc})) by the substitutions $c_1 \to -c_1$ and $c_2 \to c_2$ in (\ref{Mo7}). As expected, under this operation one has $p_{12} \leftrightarrow p_{21}$. We deduce moreover that $p_{22}=p_{11}$, which completes the picture of the two lead junction at microscopic level.
nodes.statement_short: Swapping the reservoirs exchanges $p_{12}$ and $p_{21}$ and yields $p_{22}=p_{11}$.
assumptions: by implementing $d_1 \leftrightarrow d_2$, or equivalently ... by the substitutions $c_1 \to -c_1$ and $c_2 \to c_2$ in (\ref{Mo7})

nodes.name: Normalisation of the emission-absorption probabilities
nodes.statement: It is instructive to study the behavior of the probabilities $p_{ij}$ because they provide fundamental information about the elementary processes in the system and uniquely fix the probability distribution, thus determining all moments and cumulants. Since \begin{equation} p_{11}+p_{12}+p_{21}=1\, , \end{equation} it is enough to focus on the pair $\{p_{12}, p_{21}\}$.
nodes.statement_short: The three probabilities sum to one, so only $\{p_{12},p_{21}\}$ are independent.
conclusions: it is enough to focus on the pair $\{p_{12}, p_{21}\}$

nodes.name: Low temperature limits of $p_{12}$ and $p_{21}$
nodes.statement: {}For describing the low temperature limit $\beta_1=\beta_2 \equiv \beta \to \infty$ it is convenient to adopt the variables $\mu_\pm$ defined by (\ref{mupm}), assuming without loss of generality that $\mu_-\geq 0$. Then one finds \begin{equation} \lim_{\beta \to \infty} p_{12}= \begin{cases} 0 \, , & \qquad  \mu_+ < \omega-\mu_-\, , \\ (1-\sqrt{\tau})/2\, , & \qquad \omega -\mu_- < \mu_+ < \omega + \mu_-\, , \\ 0 \, , & \qquad  \mu_+ > \omega+\mu_-\, , \\ \end{cases} \end{equation} and \begin{equation} \lim_{\beta \to \infty} p_{21}= \begin{cases} 0 \, , & \qquad  \mu_+ < \omega-\mu_-\, , \\ (1+\sqrt{\tau})/2\, , & \qquad \omega -\mu_- < \mu_+ < \omega + \mu_-\, ,\\ 0 \, , & \qquad  \mu_+ > \omega+\mu_-\, . \\ \end{cases} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: At $\beta\to\infty$ the cross probabilities are $(1\mp\sqrt\tau)/2$ inside the window $[\omega-\mu_-,\omega+\mu_-]$ and vanish outside.
assumptions: assuming without loss of generality that $\mu_-\geq 0$

nodes.name: Values at the boundary points $\mu_+=\omega\pm\mu_-$
nodes.statement: At the boundary points $\mu_+ = \omega \pm \mu_-$ one has instead \begin{eqnarray} \lim_{\beta \to \infty} p_{12}&=&(1-\sqrt{\tau})/4\, ,\qquad \lim_{\beta \to \infty} p_{21}=(1+\sqrt{\tau})/4\, ,\qquad \mu_- \not= 0 \, , \nonumber \\ \lim_{\beta \to \infty} p_{12}&=& \lim_{\beta \to \infty} p_{21}= 1/4\, ,\qquad \mu_- = 0 \, . \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: At the window edges the cross probabilities are halved, becoming $1/4$ each when $\mu_-=0$.

nodes.name: Dominance regimes of the elementary processes at low temperature
nodes.statement: We conclude that at low temperatures the process of emission and absorption from the same reservoir is favored for $\mu_+$ outside the interval $[\omega-\mu_-\, ,\, \omega+\mu_-]$, which is illustrated by the left panel of Fig. \ref{fig3}. The probabilities $p_{21}$ and $p_{12}$ are instead dominating if $\mu_+\in (\omega-\mu_-\, ,\, \omega+\mu_-)$, as shown in the right panel of the same figure. Finally, equation (\ref{b23}) implies that in the low temperature limit $p_{11}=1/2$ for $\mu_+=\omega \pm \mu_-$.
nodes.statement_short: Same-reservoir processes dominate outside the transport window, cross processes inside it, with $p_{11}=1/2$ at the edges.
conclusions: the process of emission and absorption from the same reservoir is favored for $\mu_+$ outside the interval $[\omega-\mu_-\, ,\, \omega+\mu_-]$
The probabilities $p_{21}$ and $p_{12}$ are instead dominating if $\mu_+\in (\omega-\mu_-\, ,\, \omega+\mu_-)$
in the low temperature limit $p_{11}=1/2$ for $\mu_+=\omega \pm \mu_-$

nodes.name: High temperature limit of the cross probabilities
nodes.statement: At high temperatures one has \begin{equation} \lim_{\beta\to 0} p_{12} = \lim_{\beta \to 0} p_{21} =1/4\, , \end{equation} which is manifest in Fig. \ref{fig3}.

nodes.name: High energy limit of the cross probabilities
nodes.statement: At high energies one finds \begin{equation} \lim_{\omega\to \infty} p_{12} = \lim_{\omega\to \infty} p_{21} =0\, , \end{equation} showing that in this regime the probability of emission of a particle from one reservoir and its absorption from the other one is negligible. This feature is illustrated by the blue and red curves in the plots of Fig. \ref{fig4} for constant $\tau=0.5$.
nodes.statement_short: Cross emission-absorption becomes negligible at large energy.
conclusions: in this regime the probability of emission of a particle from one reservoir and its absorption from the other one is negligible

nodes.name: Generating function in terms of the probabilities $p_{ij}$
nodes.statement: We conclude with the following two observations. First, in terms of the basic probabilities $\{p_{ij}, \tau \}$, the cumulant generating function (\ref{gf4}) takes the form \begin{eqnarray} \C (\lambda ) &=& \int_0^\infty \frac{\rd \omega}{2\pi}\, \ln \left \{1+ \ri (p_{21}-p_{12})\, \sin (\lambda  \sqrt{\tau}) + (p_{21}+p_{12})\left [\cos (\lambda  \sqrt{\tau})-1\right ] \right \} \nonumber \\ &=&\int_0^\infty \frac{\rd \omega}{2\pi}\, \ln \left [p_{11}+ p_{21}\, \e^{\ri \lambda \sqrt{\tau}} + p_{12}\, \e^{-\ri \lambda \sqrt{\tau}} \right ] \, . \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: The generating function is the energy integral of $\ln[p_{11}+p_{21}\e^{\ri\lambda\sqrt\tau}+p_{12}\e^{-\ri\lambda\sqrt\tau}]$.
assumptions: in terms of the basic probabilities $\{p_{ij}, \tau \}$

nodes.name: Multi-terminal extension of the probability distribution
nodes.statement: Second, the distribution (\ref{Mo7}) has a straightforward extension to the multi terminal system $N\geq 3$. In this case the probability distribution $\varphi (\xi)$ in the lead $L_1$ is obtained from (\ref{Mo7}) by replacing $c_i$ by the effective quantities $c_i^{\rm eff}$ according to (\ref{gf8}) and fixing $\tau$ by (\ref{gf7}). Now $p_{12}$ is the probability of the emission of a particle from $R_1$ and absorption by any of the reservoirs $\{R_2, R_3,...,R_N\}$, whereas $p_{21}$ gives the probability of the inverse process.
nodes.statement_short: For $N\ge3$ the same three-delta distribution holds with effective $c_i^{\rm eff}$ and total $\tau$.
assumptions: replacing $c_i$ by the effective quantities $c_i^{\rm eff}$ according to (\ref{gf8}) and fixing $\tau$ by (\ref{gf7})
conclusions: the distribution (\ref{Mo7}) has a straightforward extension to the multi terminal system $N\geq 3$
$p_{12}$ is the probability of the emission of a particle from $R_1$ and absorption by any of the reservoirs $\{R_2, R_3,...,R_N\}$, whereas $p_{21}$ gives the probability of the inverse process

nodes.name: Summary of the new achievements
nodes.statement: We developed a quantum field theory approach for the derivation of the $n$-point particle current correlation functions for the system in Fig. \ref{fig1}, modelling a quantum wire junction away from equilibrium. The system has the geometry of a star graph with free particle propagation along the leads and a defect interaction localised in the vertex. The new achievements in this framework are: \medskip (a) the closed and exact form (\ref{c51}-\ref{c52}) of the cumulants $\C_n$ for generic $n$; (b) the cumulant generating function (\ref{gf6}-\ref{gf8}) in the $N$-terminal case; (c) the cumulant generating function (\ref{si3}) in the scale invariant limit; (d) the moments (\ref{Mo2}) and the associated probability distribution (\ref{Mo7}); (e) the exact emission-absorption probabilities $p_{ij}$.
nodes.statement_short: Five new results: exact cumulants, $N$-terminal and scale-invariant generating functions, moments with distribution, and the $p_{ij}$.

nodes.name: Extension to Majorana fermions
nodes.statement: It will be interesting for instance to extend the above results to Majorana fermions, which attract much attention \cite{M-1,M-2} with their remarkable physical properties and potential applications in topological quantum information \cite{K-01}. In this context the quantum transport of Majorana fermions along the edge of a topological superconductor represents a fascinating problem, which can be faced by the above methods.
nodes.statement_short: Open direction: apply the framework to Majorana transport along a topological superconductor edge.

nodes.name: LB expectation values of $2n$-point functions at positive momenta
nodes.statement: In the computation of the current correlators (\ref{w1}) we need the $2n$-point functions \begin{equation} \langle a^*_{l_1}(k_1) a_{m_1}(p_1)\cdots a^*_{l_n}(k_n) a_{m_n}(p_n)\rangle_{\beta,\mu} \end{equation} for {\it positive} momenta. In this case \begin{equation} \langle a^*_{l_1}(k_1) a_{m_1}(p_1)\cdots a^*_{l_n}(k_n) a_{m_n}(p_n)\rangle_{\beta,\mu} = \frac{1}{Z} {\rm Tr} \left [\e^{-K} a^*_{l_1}(k_1) a_{m_1}(p_1)\cdots a^*_{l_n}(k_n) a_{m_n}(p_n)\right ]\, , \end{equation} where \begin{equation} K= \int_0^\infty \frac{\rd k}{2\pi} \sum_{i=1}^N \beta_i \left [\omega(k) - \mu_i\right ]a^*_i(k) a_i(k) \, , \quad Z = {\rm Tr} \left (\e^{-K}\right )\, . \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: At positive momenta the LB expectation values are Gibbs traces with $K=\int \beta_i(\omega-\mu_i)a^*_ia_i$.
nodes.section: A Correlation functions in the LB state

nodes.name: Two-point functions in the LB state
nodes.statement: {}For the two-point functions one gets ($k>0,p>0$) \begin{eqnarray} \langle a_l^*(k)a_m(p)\rangle_{\beta, \mu} &=& 2\pi \delta (k-p)\delta_{lm}d_l[\omega(k)] \equiv \Delta_{lm}(k,p)\, , \\ \langle a_m(p) a_l^*(k)\rangle_{\beta, \mu} &=& 2\pi \delta (k-p)\delta_{lm}\{1-d_l[\omega(k)]\} \equiv \widetilde{\Delta}_{lm}(k,p)\, , \end{eqnarray} where $d_l(\omega)$ is the Fermi distribution (\ref{c11}) of the reservoir $R_l$.
nodes.statement_short: The LB two-point functions are diagonal delta-functions weighted by $d_l$ and $1-d_l$.
nodes.section: A Correlation functions in the LB state

nodes.name: Determinant representation of the $2n$-point function
nodes.statement: The $2n$-point function can be expressed in terms of (\ref{A4},\ref{A5}) as a determinant. For $k_i>0,p_i>0$ one has: \begin{eqnarray} \langle a^*_{l_1}(k_1) a_{m_1}(p_1)\cdots a^*_{l_n}(k_n) a_{m_n}(p_n)\rangle_{\beta,\mu} = \qquad \qquad \quad  \nonumber \\ \left | \begin{array}{cccccccc} \Delta_{l_1m_1}(k_1,p_1)&\Delta_{l_1m_2}(k_1,p_2)&\cdots &&  \Delta_{l_1m_n}(k_1,p_n)\\ -{\widetilde{\Delta}}_{l_2m_1}(k_2,p_1)&\Delta_{l_2m_2}(k_2,p_2) & \cdots & &\Delta_{l_2m_n}(k_2,p_n) \\ \vdots &\vdots & \vdots&& \vdots \\ -{\widetilde{\Delta}}_{l_nm_1}(k_n,p_1)&-{\widetilde{\Delta}}_{l_nm_2}(k_n,p_2) & \cdots & &\Delta_{l_nm_n}(k_n,p_n)\\ \end{array}\right | \, . \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: The $2n$-point function equals a determinant built from $\Delta$ and $\widetilde\Delta$ two-point functions.
nodes.section: A Correlation functions in the LB state
conclusions: The $2n$-point function can be expressed in terms of (\ref{A4},\ref{A5}) as a determinant

nodes.name: Proof of the determinant representation by induction
nodes.statement: The validity of \eqref{A6} can be proven by induction. For $n=1$ the determinant correctly reproduces (\ref{A4}). Using the definition (\ref{A2},\ref{A3}) one can show that for $n\geq2$ \begin{equation} \langle a^*_{l_1}(k_1) a_{m_1}(p_1)\cdots a^*_{l_n}(k_n) a_{m_n}(p_n)\rangle_{\beta,\mu} = \sum_{k=1}^n \langle a^*_{l_1}(k_1) a_{m_k}(p_k)\rangle_{\beta,\mu} \langle \, \cdots \,  \rangle'_{\beta,\mu} \, , \end{equation} where the primed expectation value $\langle \, \ldots \,  \rangle'_{\beta,\mu}$ indicates that the elements $a^*_{l_1}(k_1)$ and $a_{m_k}(p_k)$ are removed from the string. Iterating this step in $\langle \, \cdots \,  \rangle'_{\beta,\mu}$ one obtains the Laplace expansion of the determinant in \eqref{A6} along the first row, which concludes the argument.
nodes.statement_short: By induction on $n$: the recursion contracting $a^*_{l_1}$ with each $a_{m_k}$ reproduces the Laplace expansion along the first row.

nodes.name: Base case $n=1$
nodes.statement: For $n=1$ the determinant correctly reproduces (\ref{A4}).
nodes.statement_short: Check the base case against the two-point function.

nodes.name: Inductive contraction identity
nodes.statement: Using the definition (\ref{A2},\ref{A3}) one can show that for $n\geq2$ \begin{equation} \langle a^*_{l_1}(k_1) a_{m_1}(p_1)\cdots a^*_{l_n}(k_n) a_{m_n}(p_n)\rangle_{\beta,\mu} = \sum_{k=1}^n \langle a^*_{l_1}(k_1) a_{m_k}(p_k)\rangle_{\beta,\mu} \langle \, \cdots \,  \rangle'_{\beta,\mu} \, , \end{equation} where the primed expectation value $\langle \, \ldots \,  \rangle'_{\beta,\mu}$ indicates that the elements $a^*_{l_1}(k_1)$ and $a_{m_k}(p_k)$ are removed from the string.
nodes.statement_short: Derive the recursion contracting $a^*_{l_1}(k_1)$ with every annihilation operator in the string.

nodes.name: Iteration yields the Laplace expansion
nodes.statement: Iterating this step in $\langle \, \cdots \,  \rangle'_{\beta,\mu}$ one obtains the Laplace expansion of the determinant in \eqref{A6} along the first row, which concludes the argument.
nodes.statement_short: Iterate the recursion and recognise the first-row Laplace expansion.

nodes.name: Reflection-transmission constraints
nodes.statement: {}Finally, one extends \cite{M-11} the correlation functions (\ref{A4}-\ref{A6}) to negative momenta by using the reflection-transmission constraints \begin{equation} a_i(k) = \sum_{j=1}^N \S_{ij}(k) a_j(-k)\, , \qquad a^*_i(k) = \sum_{j=1}^N a^*_j(-k)\S^*_{ji}(k)\, . \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Negative-momentum modes are tied to positive ones by the scattering matrix.

nodes.name: Diagonalisation of the $\T^1$ matrix
nodes.statement: The Hermitian matrices $\T^i$, defined by (\ref{T}), play a fundamental role. For illustrating their properties it is enough to focus on $\T^1$ associated with lead $L_1$. First of all, there exists a $N\times N$ unitary matrix $U$ diagonalising $\T^1$. After some algebra one finds \begin{equation} U\, \T^1\, U^* = \T^1_d  \equiv {\rm diag}[0,0,...,-\sqrt{\tau(\omega)},\sqrt{\tau(\omega)}\, ]\, , \end{equation} where \begin{equation} \tau(\omega) = \sum_{i=2}^N \tau_i (\omega)\, , \qquad  \tau_i (\omega) \equiv |\S_{i1}(\sqrt{2m\omega})|^2 \, , \end{equation} is the total transmission probability between the lead $L_1$ and the remaining leads $L_i$ with $2\leq i\leq N$. We conclude that $N-2$ of the eigenvalues of $\T^1$ vanish, the nontrivial two being $\pm \sqrt{\tau(\omega)}$.
nodes.statement_short: $\T^1$ is unitarily equivalent to ${\rm diag}[0,\dots,0,-\sqrt\tau,\sqrt\tau]$, so only two eigenvalues are nonzero.

nodes.name: Computation of the single energy channel generating function
nodes.statement: We summarise here the key points of the computation of the expectation value \eqref{fe3} which leads to the basic result \eqref{gf6}. Without loss of generality we concentrate on the lead $L_1$, the extension to other leads being straightforward. The problem consists in computing \begin{equation} \langle\e^{\ri\lambda j_\omega^1}\rangle_{\beta,\mu} = \langle \e^{\ri\lambda \sum_{i,j=1}^N a_i^*\T^1_{ij}a_j}\rangle_{\beta,\mu}\, . \end{equation} It is convenient for this purpose to change the basis in the algebra (\ref{alg}) according to \begin{equation} b_i = \sum_{j=1}^N U_{ij}\, a_j \, , \qquad b^*_i = \sum_{j=1}^N a_j^*\, U^*_{ji}\, , \end{equation} where $U$ is the matrix diagonalising $\mathbb{T}^1$ according to (\ref{Tmat1}). In the new basis the expectation value (\ref{C1}) reads \begin{equation} \langle\e^{\ri\lambda j_\omega^1}\rangle_{\beta,\mu} = \langle\prod_{j=1}^N\e^{\ri\lambda (\mathbb{T}_d^1)_{jj}b_j^*b_j}\rangle_{\beta,\mu} = \langle\prod_{j=1}^N\left[1+\left(\e^{\ri\lambda (\mathbb{T}_d^1)_{jj}}-1\right) b_j^*b_j\right]\rangle_{\beta,\mu} \, . \end{equation} In the case $N=2$ one has $\mathbb{T}^1_d={\rm diag}(-\sqrt{\tau},\sqrt{\tau})$ and one finds \begin{equation} \begin{split} \langle\e^{\ri\lambda j_\omega^1}\rangle_{\beta,\mu} &= {\rm det} \left [\II + \left (\e^{\ri \lambda \T^1_d} -\II \right ) \begin{pmatrix} \langle b^*_1b_1\rangle_{\beta,\mu} & \langle b^*_1b_2\rangle_{\beta,\mu} \\ \langle b^*_2b_1\rangle_{\beta,\mu} & \langle b^*_2b_2\rangle_{\beta,\mu} \end{pmatrix} \right ] \\ &= 1+ \ri c_1 \sqrt{\tau}\, \sin (\lambda  \sqrt{\tau}) +c_2 \left [\cos (\lambda  \sqrt{\tau})-1\right ]\, . \end{split} \end{equation} Combining (\ref{C4}) with (\ref{gf5},\ref{tgf}) one gets the final result \eqref{gf4}. The extension to a generic $N>2$ is attained by expanding the product in \eqref{C3} and expressing the multiple correlators of the operators $\lbrace b_i,b_i^*\rbrace$ in terms of two-point functions through the analogue of formula \eqref{A6}. One recognises at this point that the series can be re-summed as a determinant \begin{equation} \langle\e^{\ri\lambda j_\omega^1}\rangle_{\beta,\mu} = {\rm det} \left [\II + \left (\e^{\ri \lambda \T^1} -\II \right ) \D \right ]\, , \end{equation} where $\D$ is the diagonal matrix (\ref{m1}) of the Fermi distributions of the reservoirs. In the basis in which $\T^1$ is diagonal the result (\ref{C5}) takes the form \begin{equation} \langle\e^{\ri\lambda j_\omega^1}\rangle_{\beta,\mu} = {\rm det} \left [\II + \left (\e^{\ri \lambda \T_d^1} -\II \right ) U\, \D\, U^*\right ]\, . \end{equation} Using the explicit form of $U$, which can be deduced from (\ref{Tmat3}, \ref{Tmat4}), one obtains from (\ref{C6}) the cumulant generating function (\ref{gf6} - \ref{gf8}) in the multi terminal case.
nodes.statement_short: Diagonalise $\T^1$, factorise the exponential over the new fermionic modes, evaluate $N=2$ explicitly and re-sum the general case into a determinant.
